Scott Kimball told his wife that his uncle had won the lottery and left for Mexico with a stripper, the affidavit said, but FBI investigators think Kimball killed his uncle and dumped his body in Vail Pass, more than 100 miles from the home they shared in a Denver suburb. In March, Kimball accompanied FBI investigators to southeastern Utah to search for the body of Leann Emry, who was 24 when she vanished after departing on a camping trip in 2003. FBI agents found Emry's remains shortly after Kimball returned to jail. Kaysi McLeod was 19 when she disappeared in 2003. McLeod, the daughter of Kimball's ex-wife, was last seen getting a ride to work from Kimball, according to the 2007 affidavit. In fall 2007, a hunter found her remains in northwest Colorado. Kimball is also suspected in the disappearance of exotic dancer Jennifer Marcum, who disappeared in 2003, according to the affidavit. "We are continuing to look for Jennifer, and we will leave no stone unturned," Wright said. Kimball drew the FBI's attention in 2002 while jailed for writing bad checks. On Monday, searchers discovered partially mummified bones in an isolated Rocky Mountain pass near Vail, Colorado. Authorities believe the remains may belong to Kimball’s uncle, Terry Kimball. According to law enforcement sources close to the case, Kimball told authorities earlier this year where they could find remains believed to be those of his uncle. Snow prevented an immediate search, so investigators waited for it to melt.

The FBI declined to verify that Kimball had directed agents to the location. FBI spokeswoman Kathleen Wright did say, however, “We went to (a) specific location for a specific reason. It wasn’t random.”

Terry Kimball, who was 60, was last observed with his nephew in September 2004, according to an affidavit supporting a 2007 federal search warrant. Scott Kimball later told his wife that Terry had won the lottery and traveled to Mexico with a stripper. Kimball has also assisted authorities in another case. In March, he traveled with FBI investigators to southeastern Utah as they searched for Leann Emry, who disappeared in 2003 at age 24 after leaving for a camping trip. Agents located Emry’s remains soon after Kimball was returned to prison.

Another case involves Kaysi McLeod, the daughter of Kimball’s former wife. She was 19 when she vanished in 2003. The 2007 affidavit states that she was last seen accepting a ride to work from Kimball. A hunter discovered her remains in northwestern Colorado during the fall of 2007.

Investigators also suspect Kimball in the 2003 disappearance of exotic dancer Jennifer Marcum, according to the affidavit. Sources familiar with the inquiry believe he murdered Marcum and buried her near Rifle, Colorado, but her body has not been recovered.

“We are continuing to look for Jennifer, and we will leave no stone unturned,” Wright said.

Kimball first came to the FBI’s attention in 2002, when he was in jail for passing bad checks. **DENVER (CNN-style report)** — Convicted murderer Scott Lee Kimball led investigators to remote areas of Colorado and Utah where authorities recovered the remains of several people linked to his killing spree, officials said.

Kimball, a former FBI informant with a long criminal history, provided information that helped law enforcement search isolated mountain and desert locations for people who disappeared after he was released from prison in 2002.

The victims connected to Kimball included 19-year-old Kaysi McLeod, 24-year-old LeAnn Emry, 25-year-old Jennifer Marcum and Kimball’s uncle, Terry Kimball. Their disappearances occurred in 2003 and 2004.

Search teams recovered remains in rugged areas of Colorado and Utah, and investigators used dental records, DNA testing and other forensic evidence to identify some of the victims. Marcum’s remains have not been found.

Kimball pleaded guilty in 2009 to four counts of second-degree murder and received a 70-year prison sentence. As part of the plea agreement, he admitted killing the four victims and agreed to provide investigators with information about where their bodies had been left.

The case drew particular scrutiny because Kimball had been released from prison to work as an FBI informant. While free, he committed fraud and carried out the killings, according to prosecutors.

Authorities have continued examining Kimball’s movements and statements to determine whether he could be connected to other unsolved disappearances or deaths. Investigators have said any additional claims must be independently verified because Kimball has a history of deception.

For the victims’ families, the recovery and identification of remains offered answers after years of uncertainty, though the search for Marcum has continued.

counterfactuals.output:
**Why suspected serial killer Scott Kimball initially appeared unlikely to face homicide charges**

**DENVER —** Investigators came to believe that Scott Lee Kimball was responsible for several deaths and disappearances in Colorado and the West, but for years prosecutors faced a familiar obstacle in suspected serial-murder cases: suspicion, even strong suspicion, is not enough to prove homicide beyond a reasonable doubt.

Kimball, a convicted con man who briefly worked as an FBI informant after being released from prison in 2002, was linked to four people who vanished between 2003 and 2004: Kaysi McLeod, Jennifer Marcum, LeAnn Emry and Kimball’s uncle, Terry Kimball. The circumstances surrounding the disappearances, Kimball’s relationships with the victims and information he allegedly supplied to investigators made him the central suspect.

Yet authorities initially warned that murder charges might not be possible.

The principal problem was the condition—or absence—of the victims’ remains. Marcum’s body was never recovered, while other remains were discovered in remote areas or only identified after significant time had passed. Exposure, decomposition and the passage of years can destroy evidence needed to establish the cause and manner of death. Without that evidence, prosecutors can struggle to prove not only who killed a victim, but whether a legally provable homicide occurred at all.

A missing-person case can be prosecuted without a body, but such cases generally require a strong chain of circumstantial evidence: proof that the victim is dead, evidence placing the defendant with the victim, a demonstrated motive, incriminating statements, physical evidence, or conduct showing an effort to conceal the crime. In Kimball’s case, investigators had suspicious patterns and connections, but much of the publicly known evidence was indirect.

Kimball also reportedly gave shifting accounts and led investigators to locations associated with the victims. Such statements can help police, but they do not automatically produce a viable prosecution. Prosecutors must determine whether a statement is admissible, corroborated and sufficiently reliable. Information obtained through Kimball’s role as an informant also raised potential complications, including what promises had been made to him and whether defense lawyers could challenge the government’s handling of him.

His informant status did not give him blanket immunity from murder charges. It did, however, threaten to complicate a trial. A defense could scrutinize the FBI’s decision to secure his release, its supervision of him and any agreements governing his cooperation. Authorities would also have had to separate admissible evidence from information obtained under particular cooperation arrangements.

In addition, investigators had to build separate cases for each victim. Evidence suggesting a common pattern can be important, but prosecutors ordinarily must prove every charged killing independently. A jury’s belief that a defendant is generally dangerous or connected to several disappearances cannot substitute for proof of a specific homicide.

Those difficulties explain why authorities at one stage considered relying on charges that were easier to document, including fraud, escape and weapons offenses. Such charges could keep Kimball in custody while investigators continued searching for remains and corroborating evidence. They also provided leverage in negotiations without forcing prosecutors to risk an acquittal in a prematurely filed murder case.

The legal picture ultimately changed. Investigators recovered and identified remains, developed additional evidence and negotiated a resolution. In 2009, Kimball pleaded guilty in Colorado to four counts of second-degree murder in the deaths of McLeod, Marcum, Emry and Terry Kimball. He received a 70-year state sentence, consecutive to a federal sentence he was already serving.

Thus, the concern that Kimball might never be charged reflected the evidentiary state of the cases at an earlier point—not a conclusion that authorities lacked suspicion or that his work as an informant protected him. The delay demonstrated the gap prosecutors must bridge between identifying a likely killer and assembling evidence strong enough to support homicide convictions.

counterfactuals.output:
# From FBI Informant to Convicted Killer: The Scott Kimball Investigation

Scott Lee Kimball spent years moving between prisons, courtrooms and fraudulent schemes before emerging as a central figure in four disappearances and murders across Colorado and neighboring states.

What made the case especially troubling was Kimball’s relationship with the FBI. After cultivating him as a confidential informant in a drug investigation, federal authorities helped secure his release from custody in late 2002. Over the next two years, four people connected to Kimball vanished or were killed.

The FBI and local agencies later faced the difficult task of retracing the movements of a man who had repeatedly lied to investigators—and who understood how law enforcement worked.

## A long record of fraud and deception

Before he was investigated for homicide, Kimball had accumulated an extensive criminal history involving fraud, forgery, theft and other financial crimes. He used aliases, passed bad checks and created elaborate stories to manipulate relatives, romantic partners and authorities.

Kimball’s talent for deception helped make him useful as an informant. While incarcerated, he offered information about another prisoner and a purported criminal plot. The FBI began working with him, and a federal judge authorized his release so he could assist investigators.

The decision gave Kimball access to potential victims at a time when he remained under federal supervision. Later reviews found serious weaknesses in how he was monitored, although Kimball himself was responsible for the crimes to which he ultimately pleaded guilty.

## Four people disappear

The cases linked to Kimball unfolded between 2003 and 2004.

### LeAnn Emry

LeAnn Emry, 24, disappeared in January 2003. Kimball had become involved with her shortly before she vanished. Her remains were later found in a remote area of Utah, but they were not identified until years afterward.

Investigators said Kimball misled people about Emry’s whereabouts and gave conflicting accounts of what had happened to her. Her case eventually became one of the four killings included in his murder plea.

### Jennifer Marcum

Jennifer Marcum, 25, disappeared in February 2003. She had a particularly complicated connection to Kimball: he had provided information to the FBI about Marcum’s boyfriend, who had been incarcerated with him, and Kimball later became involved with Marcum’s mother.

Marcum was last known to be in the Denver area. Kimball offered shifting explanations about her disappearance, but investigators concluded that he killed her. Her body has never been recovered, leaving her family without a burial site and authorities without a complete account of the crime.

### Kaysi McLeod

Kaysi McLeod, 19, was Kimball’s stepdaughter. She disappeared in August 2003 after spending time with him.

Kimball initially claimed McLeod had left voluntarily, one of several stories he used to delay scrutiny. Her remains were eventually discovered in a remote part of northern Colorado. The recovery gave investigators physical evidence tying another missing-person case to Kimball’s circle.

### Terry Kimball

Terry Kimball, Scott Kimball’s uncle, disappeared in 2004. His remains were later found near Vail Pass in Colorado.

As in the other cases, Scott Kimball gave relatives misleading accounts about the victim’s location and condition. The death of a family member underscored that Kimball’s victims were not confined to one type of relationship; they included a girlfriend, a young woman linked to his informant work, a stepdaughter and an uncle.

## The investigation closes in

Kimball’s financial crimes eventually helped bring him back into custody. Investigators examining his fraud and forgery uncovered inconsistencies surrounding the missing people in his life. Local police, sheriff’s offices and federal agents began comparing timelines, interviews and physical evidence across jurisdictions.

The inquiry was complicated by the remote locations where victims had been left, the delay in identifying some remains and Kimball’s repeated efforts to send investigators in the wrong direction. Authorities also had to revisit information he had supplied while serving as an FBI source and determine what had been genuine and what had been designed to protect himself.

In 2009, Kimball pleaded guilty in Colorado state court to four counts of second-degree murder in the deaths of Emry, Marcum, McLeod and Terry Kimball. He received a 70-year prison sentence under an agreement intended, in part, to resolve the cases without separate trials.

## Scrutiny of the FBI’s handling of Kimball

The case prompted criticism of the FBI’s management of confidential informants. Kimball had a substantial record of dishonesty, yet he was released and allowed to operate in the community while providing information to federal agents. Three of the victims disappeared within roughly a year of that release, and the fourth vanished the following year.

Federal reviews concluded that agents had not adequately supervised Kimball or fully recognized the risk he posed. The episode became a cautionary example of the danger involved when authorities rely on criminal informants whose usefulness may obscure their capacity for further violence.

Kimball’s convictions resolved the question of criminal responsibility in court, but important uncertainties remain—most notably the location of Jennifer Marcum’s body and whether Kimball gave investigators a complete account of his crimes.

The case endures not only as the story of a practiced con man who became a serial murderer, but also as a warning about the consequences of misplaced confidence in an informant skilled at exploiting the people assigned to control him.
